Solvent cage

Words: 26
Physical chemistry OurBigBook.com
The surrounding solvent environment that temporarily keeps newly separated reaction fragments near one another. Geminate recombination can retain ligand identity even after a metal-ligand bond breaks.

Hammett equation (log(kX​/kH​)=ρσX​)

Words: 20
Physical chemistry OurBigBook.com
The linear free-energy relation log(kX​/kH​)=ρσX​. The substituent constant measures electronic character and the reaction constant measures its kinetic sensitivity.

Electrophoresis

Words: 291 Articles: 5
Physical chemistry OurBigBook.com
Electrophoresis is motion of charged dispersed species relative to a surrounding medium under an applied electric field. The drift depends on electrical driving and friction, including the surrounding ionic atmosphere. Gel electrophoresis adds a porous matrix that makes migration sensitive to molecular size and conformation.

Gel sieving of synthetic polymers

Words: 69
Electrophoresis OurBigBook.com
A porous gel changes the electrophoretic mobility of charged synthetic polymers through confinement, deformation and pore-to-pore dynamics. Free-draining charge and friction can both grow proportionally to chain length, leaving free-solution mobility nearly length independent; matrix obstruction adds size sensitivity. reptation supplies one weak-field long-chain regime, not a universal calibration. Matrix concentration, effective charge, solvent conditions, conformation, topology, adsorption, electro-osmotic drift and heating can all alter migration. Size standards should match the relevant chemistry and operating regime.

Diffusive broadening of electrophoretic bands (σ2(t)=σ02​+2Dt)

Words: 93
Electrophoresis OurBigBook.com
A narrow population band undergoing uniform electrophoresis and ordinary diffusion has mean position x0​+μEt and variance σ02​+2Dt. This follows from the advection-diffusion equation by changing to the coordinate x−μEt. For two species with mobility difference Δμ, their centre separation is ∣Δμ∣Et, whereas diffusion widths grow only as t​. Starting from point-like bands with common diffusion coefficient D, a required separation of q standard deviations needs
t≥(ΔμE)22q2D​.
(1)
A prescribed distance between centres alone is a resolution convention; finite loading widths and other dispersion mechanisms must be included when interpreting actual electrophoresis data.

Electrophoretic mobility (v=μE)

Words: 88 Articles: 2
Electrophoresis OurBigBook.com
The electrophoretic mobility μ is the proportionality coefficient between drift velocity and a weak applied electric field. Its sign specifies motion relative to the field. When only travel distances are used, the mobility magnitude is often intended. For long linear DNA in a weak-field reptation regime, ∣μ∣ can scale inversely with chain length, whereas free-solution mobility is approximately length-independent. Neither law supplies a universal gel electrophoresis size calibration for arbitrary gel concentration, field strength or molecular topology.

Hückel electrophoretic mobility (μe​=2ϵζ/(3η))

Words: 10
Electrophoretic mobility OurBigBook.com
The small-particle, thick-double-layer approximation μe​=2ϵζ/(3η) under its linear electrokinetic assumptions.

Smoluchowski electrophoretic mobility (μe​=ϵζ/η)

Words: 11
Electrophoretic mobility OurBigBook.com
The thin-double-layer approximation μe​=ϵζ/η, neglecting important relaxation and surface-conduction corrections.

Crystal structure

Words: 6k Articles: 138
Physical chemistry OurBigBook.com Tags: Solid
A crystal structure specifies the chemical species and spatial arrangement of the chemical atoms or ions in a crystal. For an ideal periodic structure, separate two ingredients: a Bravais lattice specifies the translations that repeat the arrangement, and an atomic basis of a crystal specifies the chemical motif repeated at every lattice point. The outward shape, or crystal habit, is a different description: the internal arrangement is what this article describes.
For a concrete two-dimensional model, choose primitive lattice translation vectors a1​=(2,0) and a2​=(0,1.5) in arbitrary length units. At every lattice point R=ma1​+na2​, with integers m,n, place species A at R and a different species B at R+(0.65,0.55). Translating by a1​ or a2​ preserves both the positions and their chemical labels. Translating by (0.65,0.55) sends one A position to a B position, so it is not a translation symmetry of the labeled structure. A picture of dots with the labels erased can therefore conceal essential chemical information.
A primitive unit cell contains one lattice point, but may contain several chemical atoms. A conventional unit cell can contain several lattice points to display the symmetry more clearly. Thus the conventional cube of a face-centered cubic lattice contains four lattice points, whereas a body-centered cubic lattice has two. Neither lattice name alone specifies which chemical species occupies the repeated motif. The NaCl conventional cell and coordination example makes the distinction explicit.
This separation is useful experimentally: interplanar spacings constrain the repeating geometry, while relative wave intensities also depend on the atomic basis of a crystal through the crystal basis structure factor. The Bragg crystal reflection experiment of 1913 describes the X-ray spectrometer, angular scans and detector checks in detail. Its conversion from angle to length is developed under Bragg's law; a geometrically possible reflection can still have zero wave intensity.
William Lawrence Bragg's 1913 structure determination supplied a complementary test. He directed X-rays through sodium chloride sections cut parallel to a cube face and recorded spots on photographic plates. Comparing section thicknesses tested how transmission altered the pattern: the relative spot strengths changed. Comparing related salts led him to two interpenetrating face-centered cubic lattices, one for each kind of constituent. He explicitly distinguished evidence for that arrangement from the still-needed identification of a single chemical atom with each scattering center. The photographs were evidence for a structural model, not direct pictures of labeled ions.[ref]

Hard-sphere cubic packing fractions (ηFCC​=π/(32​),ηBCC​=3​π/8)

Words: 55
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
Nearest touching spheres on an FCC conventional cell meet along face diagonals, giving 4r=2​a and four spheres per cell. In BCC they meet along body diagonals, giving 4r=3​a and two spheres per cell. Dividing the respective sphere volumes by a3 proves the displayed packing fractions. A coordination-number comparison alone does not calculate the occupied volume.

Hexagonal unit-cell volume (Vcell​=3​a2c/2)

Words: 44
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
For basal vectors of equal length a separated by120degrees and perpendicular height c, cell volume is a2csin120∘=3​a2c/2. A full hexagonal prism drawn around it has three times this volume and must contain three times as many atoms if used for density calculations.

Tetrahedral interstitial site

Words: 37
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
A position surrounded by four nearest sites at tetrahedron vertices. A conventional face-centred cubic cell has eight such sites, at all combinations of quarter and three-quarter fractional coordinates. Whether occupancy constitutes a defect depends on the reference crystal.

Cubic close-packed structure

Words: 9
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
A one-atom close-packed structure with a face-centered cubic lattice and ABCABC… close-packed stacking sequence.

Close-packed stacking sequence

Words: 22
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
The sequence of lateral positions of triangular atomic layers. Cubic close packing has ABCABC… stacking and hexagonal close packing has ABAB… stacking.

Crystal interface

Words: 97 Articles: 5
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
A boundary between crystalline regions or phases. Its excess free energy depends on orientation, chemical bonding and lattice matching.

Interfacial energy (γ)

Words: 12
Crystal interface OurBigBook.com
The excess free energy per interface area, specified for the phases, orientation, temperature and constraints.

Incoherent crystal interface

Words: 18
Crystal interface OurBigBook.com
An interface without extended one-to-one lattice registry; its local structure and energy differ from those of a coherent crystal interface.

Semicoherent crystal interface

Words: 12
Crystal interface OurBigBook.com
An interface with largely matched regions separated by a network of misfit dislocations.

Coherent crystal interface

Words: 38 Articles: 1
Crystal interface OurBigBook.com
An interface whose lattice planes match continuously across the boundary. Elastic misfit strain can accumulate when the unstrained lattice parameters differ.
Coherency strain
Words: 22
Coherent crystal interface OurBigBook.com
Elastic deformation required to match differing natural lattice spacings across a coherent crystal interface. Its energy can affect precipitate shape and loss of coherency.

Diamond cubic structure

Words: 148 Articles: 3
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
An FCC Bravais lattice with a two-atom basis at fractional positions (0,0,0) and (1/4,1/4,1/4). Its conventional cubic cell contains eight atoms. Equal scattering amplitudes at the two basis sites produce additional systematic absences beyond the FCC parity selection rule.

Hard-sphere packing fraction of diamond cubic (f=π3​/16)

Words: 35
Diamond cubic structure OurBigBook.com
Nearest neighbors are separated by a3​/4, so touching spheres have radius a3​/8. Eight atoms in a conventional cell occupy fraction π3​/16≃0.3401. The underlying FCC Bravais lattice does not make this two-atom network close packed.

Bond-centred inversion in diamond cubic ((1/8,1/8,1/8))

Words: 32
Diamond cubic structure OurBigBook.com
The point (1/8,1/8,1/8) is an inversion centre when an atom is at the origin. Inversion sends r to (1/4,1/4,1/4)−r and exchanges the identical FCC sublattices. The individual atomic sites are not inversion centres.

Vertical mirrors of the diamond cubic structure (x±y=n/2)

Words: 45
Diamond cubic structure OurBigBook.com
With one atom at the origin and the second FCC sublattice displaced by (1/4,1/4,1/4), the vertical mirrors normal to directions perpendicular to [001] have traces x−y=n/2 or x+y=n/2 in fractional coordinates. Checking the atomic heights distinguishes a genuine mirror from a misleading planar projection.

Crystal motif

Words: 38
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
The arrangement of atoms or other constituents attached identically to every lattice point of a Bravais lattice. The lattice specifies translations; the motif specifies the contents repeated by those translations. A multi-atom motif does not make its atoms separate lattice points.

Hexagonal close-packed structure

Words: 19
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
A close-packed structure with hexagonal symmetry. Its basal and c-axis directions need not have equal thermal or irradiation response.

Orthorhombic crystal system

Words: 53 Articles: 1
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
A crystal system with three mutually perpendicular axes that are not constrained by symmetry to have equal lengths.

C-centered orthorhombic lattice

Words: 35
Orthorhombic crystal system OurBigBook.com
A Bravais lattice with three perpendicular conventional axes and lattice points at (0,0,0) and (1/2,1/2,0). A translation by half a diagonal of an ab face preserves the complete crystal motif; apparent centering of unlabelled molecular centers alone is insufficient.

Pyrochlore structure

Words: 21
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
An ordered, anion-deficient fluorite-related structure often written A2​B2​O7​. It can accommodate compositions and cation sizes outside the stability range of zirconolite polytypes.

Polytype

Words: 20
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
A structural variant differing in the stacking sequence of closely related layers. zirconolite polytypes can change as substituted-ion size and composition change.

L10 crystal structure (L10​)

Words: 42
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
An ordered binary structure with alternating species layers along a tetragonal axis. In primitive tetragonal coordinates one species can occupy (0,0,0) and the other (1/2,1/2,1/2). The latter vector exchanges species and therefore is not a translation of the chemically ordered crystal.

Crystallographic texture

Words: 21
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
A nonuniform distribution of crystallographic orientations among grains in a polycrystal. It can turn directional single-crystal properties into directional bulk behavior.

Lattice constant

Words: 17
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
A length parameter specifying a periodic unit cell. A conventional cubic edge is not always the nearest-neighbour distance.

Perovskite structure

Words: 14
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
An ABX3 connectivity of corner-sharing BX6 octahedra with A ions in the larger cavities.

Wurtzite

Words: 32
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
A hexagonal tetrahedrally coordinated structure with ABAB stacking of the relevant bilayers, contrasted with ABCABC stacking in zinc blende. It can occur as a nanowire polytype even when bulk conditions favour another phase.

Stacking fault

Words: 21
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
A local interruption of the normal sequence of close-packed or other crystallographic layers. It can change local symmetry and influence nanocrystal growth.

Crystal twinning

Words: 73 Articles: 1
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
An orientation relationship between adjacent crystalline regions related by a specific crystallographic symmetry operation. A multiply twinned particle is not one perfect lattice with the composite particle symmetry.

Multiply twinned particle

Words: 45
Crystal twinning OurBigBook.com
A finite particle composed of several crystallographically twinned domains. A composite fivefold outline does not require one periodic lattice to have fivefold rotational symmetry. In a decahedral fcc model, five tetrahedral domains meet around a common near-⟨110⟩ axis; elastic distortion accommodates the angular deficit.

Zone axis

Words: 54 Articles: 1
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
A crystallographic direction shared by a set of planes. Aligning a transmission electron microscopy beam along a suitable zone axis can excite multiple useful lattice reflections.

Zone law (hu+kv+lw=0)

Words: 33
Zone axis OurBigBook.com
The reciprocal vector of a plane containing the real-space direction [uvw] is perpendicular to that direction, giving hu+kv+lw=0 in consistent crystallographic indexing. For a cubic [110] zone, allowed plane indices satisfy h+k=0.

Crystal orientation

Words: 18
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
The orientation of a crystal structure relative to a specimen or instrument coordinate frame. It determines which Bragg diffraction conditions are excited.

L12 structure (L12​)

Words: 29
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
An ordered cubic A3​B structure with B at cube corners and A at face centres. The chemically labelled Bravais lattice is primitive cubic; its superlattice reflections distinguish it from a chemically disordered face-centered cubic lattice.

Caesium chloride structure

Words: 42
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
A binary crystal structure with one species at the corners of a primitive cubic unit cell and the other at its body centre. Each species has coordination number eight. Distinct chemical labels mean that the body-centre translation is not a translation symmetry; its Bravais lattice is primitive cubic, not body-centred cubic.

Fluorite structure

Words: 66 Articles: 1
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
An AB2​ crystal structure with A on a face-centered cubic lattice and B occupying all eight tetrahedral sites of its conventional cubic unit cell. The coordination numbers are eight for A and four for B. The cubic cell contains four AB2​ formula units.

Fluorite packing fraction (η)

Words: 32
Fluorite structure OurBigBook.com
With anion radius ra​, cation radius rc​ and unlike-neighbour contact, the conventional cell gives η=(π3​/4)(rc3​+2ra3​)/(rc​+ra​)3. At the eight-coordinate limiting contact ratio this is π(33​−4)/6. The cation-contact tetrahedral-hole limit is a different geometric ideal.

Tetragonal crystal system

Words: 75 Articles: 1
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
A crystal system with mutually perpendicular conventional cell axes and lengths a=b=c. The physical length of the direction [uvw] is proportional to a2(u2+v2)+c2w2​; crystallographic indices are coefficients in a lattice basis, not necessarily Cartesian components of equal scale.

Primitive tetragonal lattice

Words: 36
Tetragonal crystal system OurBigBook.com
A Bravais lattice with mutually perpendicular primitive vectors of lengths a,a,c, with c=a. A chemically ordered L10 crystal structure has this translation lattice even when drawn using a larger four-site cell that resembles a distorted FCC conventional cell.

Crystallographic defect

Words: 2k Articles: 52
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
A crystallographic defect is a departure from ideal repeated structure. In an ionic crystal, a missing ion can provide an available site for another ion to move into; movement still requires overcoming an activation energy. This is why an ideal immobile-site model is a limit rather than a universal law for solid electrical conductivity.[ref]

Antiphase boundary

Words: 43
Crystallographic defect OurBigBook.com
An interface between ordered domains related by a displacement that is a translation of the underlying disordered lattice but not of the ordered chemical structure. Slip by that displacement can leave an antiphase boundary behind a dislocation; a second appropriate displacement can restore the order.

Grain boundary

Words: 75 Articles: 2
Crystallographic defect OurBigBook.com
An interface between crystalline regions with different orientations. Its structure affects transport, mechanical response and absorption of mobile point defects.
Grain boundary strengthening
Words: 56 Articles: 1
Grain boundary OurBigBook.com
Resistance to plastic flow associated with grain boundaries obstructing or transmitting dislocations. In the ordinary Hall-Petch regime, smaller grains raise the yield stress, but at high temperature the same boundaries can accelerate diffusion creep.
Hall-Petch relation (σy​=σ0​+ky​d−1/2)
Words: 26
Grain boundary strengthening OurBigBook.com
The empirical scaling σy​=σ0​+ky​d−1/2 of yield stress with average grain size in its applicable regime. It is not a universal law for arbitrarily small grains or high-temperature deformation.

Point defect

Words: 184 Articles: 7
Crystallographic defect OurBigBook.com
A localized crystal defect such as a vacancy, substitutional impurity or interstitial atom.
Graphene vacancy defect
Words: 80 Articles: 2
Point defect OurBigBook.com
A missing carbon-atom inventory in graphene. Local reconstruction changes the nearby ring pattern and electronic states; irradiation and subsequent annealing can change the reconstruction.
Graphene divacancy
Words: 26
Graphene vacancy defect OurBigBook.com
A graphene vacancy defect with two carbon atoms removed. A common adjacent-pair reconstruction has a 5–8–5 ring arrangement; other reconstructed arrangements exist and can be selected by energetic processing.
Graphene monovacancy
Words: 30
Graphene vacancy defect OurBigBook.com
A graphene vacancy defect with one carbon removed. A common reconstruction has a pentagon and nine-membered ring with residual under-coordination. The reconstructed geometry need not retain the symmetry of the unrelaxed missing-atom site.
Self-interstitial
Words: 24
Point defect OurBigBook.com
An extra atom of the host material accommodated outside the ordinary lattice-site inventory. It can migrate, recombine with a vacancy, or join a cluster.
Vacancy
Words: 42 Articles: 1
Point defect OurBigBook.com
An unoccupied site in an otherwise specified crystal structure. Equilibrium vacancies and an irradiation-driven vacancy supersaturation have different origins.
Vacancy supersaturation (cv​>cveq​)
Words: 26
Vacancy OurBigBook.com
A vacancy population above its thermal-equilibrium value at the specified temperature. It can drive net vacancy absorption by growing cavities when competing sinks and emission permit.
Frenkel pair
Words: 25
Point defect OurBigBook.com
A vacancy and a displaced atom occupying an interstitial position. Recombination restores the occupied lattice site; spatial separation or trapping can allow the defects to survive.

Kröger–Vink notation

Words: 18
Crystallographic defect OurBigBook.com
Notation specifying a defect species, its lattice site and its charge relative to the corresponding ideal lattice site.

Carbon nanotube vacancy defect

Words: 29
Crystallographic defect OurBigBook.com
A missing carbon atom or group of atoms in a carbon nanotube wall. Local reconstruction can produce a 5–9 monovacancy or 5–8–5 divacancy ring inventory; larger vacancies can interrupt a shell.

Stone-Wales defect

Words: 22
Crystallographic defect OurBigBook.com
A bond rotation that changes four hexagons in a graphitic carbon network into a pentagon-heptagon-heptagon-pentagon ring arrangement without adding or removing atoms.

Dislocation

Words: 912 Articles: 30
Crystallographic defect OurBigBook.com
A line defect in a crystal structure. Its Burgers vector measures the closure failure of a circuit around the line. Motion can produce permanent plasticity without simultaneously breaking every bond across a whole plane.
Dislocation line-tension estimate (Tℓ​∼Gb2)
Words: 45
Dislocation OurBigBook.com

Words: 297 Articles: 4
Crystallographic defect OurBigBook.com
A missing atom at a lattice site that would be occupied in the reference crystal. A vacancy defect is a point defect and can contribute configurational entropy because many choices of empty sites can have the same macroscopic energy. Formation energy and pressure-volume work oppose this entropy gain. Vacancies can be present in thermal equilibrium; they need not all be preparation mistakes. Their allowed number and creation mechanism depend on whether the lattice size, atom number and surface reservoirs are fixed.

An unoccupied oxygen site in a reference crystal structure. Removing an oxide ion gives an effective charge +2e relative to the perfect lattice; the charge of the actual missing ion is −2e. A physical sample must satisfy overall charge neutrality through other defects, electronic carriers or changed cation valences.
Equilibrium vacancies with variable lattice size (n∗​≃N/[e(ϵ+pv)/(kB​T)−1])
Words: 166 Articles: 1
Vacancy defect OurBigBook.com
Consider fixed N atoms and variable n vacancies among N+n sites, each of volume v, with vacancy energy ϵ. The configuration count is (N+n)!/(N!n!). At fixed pressure and temperature, leading Stirling's approximation gives the excess Gibbs free energy n(ϵ+pv)−kB​T[(N+n)ln(N+n)−NlnN−nlnn]. Its stationary point is the displayed n∗​, and its second derivative is kB​TN/[n(N+n)]>0. Relative to the vacancy-free Gibbs free energy, the minimum is NkB​Tln(1−e−(ϵ+pv)/(kB​T)). The resulting mean-field volume is v(N+n∗​). Normalizability requires ϵ+pv>0, and large vacancy fractions lie outside a realistic dilute-defect crystal model.

Equilibrium vacancies with variable lattice size OurBigBook.com
If the variable-site model counts every n sector with weight (nN+n​)qn, its exact relative partition sum is (1−q)−N−1. Differentiating its logarithm gives the displayed exact mean. Minimizing the leading extensive Gibbs free energy instead gives Nq/(1−q), the same result to relative order 1/N. Its exact relative equilibrium free energy is (N+1)kB​Tln(1−q). This correction distinguishes a thermodynamic saddle from an exact finite-system average; changing the microscopic site-creation convention can also change subextensive factors.

X-ray crystallographic structure inference

Words: 1k Articles: 4
Crystallography OurBigBook.com
X-ray crystallographic structure inference is an inverse problem: infer a crystal structure from measured X-ray diffraction. A proposed unit cell and atomic basis of a crystal predict a pattern; structure determination asks which proposals survive comparison with that pattern. The useful separation is between directions and strengths. Peak positions constrain the reciprocal lattice and hence interplanar spacings; relative wave intensities constrain the motif through the crystal basis structure factor. Knowing a repeat distance does not locate all the chemical atoms within that repeat.
The lattice constant from two indexed reflections example isolates the geometric inference. Basis intensities and phase ambiguity then holds the translations fixed while changing the motif. Even complete, noiseless wave intensity data need not determine all wave phases: this is the phase problem. Chemical composition, symmetry, and additional measurements can supply constraints beyond the original pattern.[ref]
Lattice constant from two indexed reflections
Words: 313
X-ray crystallographic structure inference OurBigBook.com
Choose an original simulated model: a primitive cubic lattice with one identical point scatterer per primitive unit cell, edge a=0.400nm, and incident X-ray wavelength λ=0.200nm. These are stipulated lengths, not measurements of sodium chloride. Suppose orientation information has already assigned the two observed reflections the Miller indices (100) and (110). The detector deflection is 2θ, where θ is the Bragg angle.
Use the existing interplanar spacing formula and Bragg's law, with higher diffraction orders absorbed into the reflection indices:
N=h2+k2+l2,dhkl​=N​a​,sin2θhkl​=4a2λ2​N,a=2sinθhkl​λN​​.
(2)
The simulated (100) reflection has sinθ=1/4, hence 2θ=28.9550∘. The (110) reflection has sinθ=2​/4, hence 2θ=41.4096∘. Their squared sines are 0.0625 and 0.125, in ratio 1:2. Substituting the unrounded angles independently gives
a100​=2(1/4)0.200​=0.400nm,a110​=2(2​/4)0.2002​​=0.400nm.
(3)
Agreement tests a proposed indexing and scale together; disagreement would prompt checks of the indexing, wavelength, angular zero, or the assumed unit cell geometry.
Two peak positions alone do not establish the indexing. Assigning the same two angles to (110) and (200) would give N=2,4 and a=0.4002​≃0.565685nm instead. More reflections, orientation information and systematic absences help discriminate such assignments. An unobserved reflection can be inaccessible, weak or extinguished by the atomic basis; absence is not automatically evidence for a larger interplanar spacing.
Absolute scale also requires measurement calibration of the wavelength. To first order, differentiation of the inferred length gives
aδa​=λδλ​−cotθδθ,
(4)
with angular changes in radians. A stipulated detector-zero error δ(2θ)=+0.100∘, with correct wavelength, biases the first inferred edge downward by approximately 0.338% and the second by 0.231%. A common angular offset therefore need not cancel when two inferred lengths are compared. These are model sensitivity estimates, not historical instrument uncertainties.
Basis intensities and phase ambiguity
Words: 303
X-ray crystallographic structure inference OurBigBook.com
Keep the cubic translations above, but attach an atomic basis with A at fractional crystal coordinates (0,0,0) and B at (u,0,0). Stipulate real, angle-independent relative scattering amplitudes fA​=1 and fB​=0.6. Neglect wave absorption, repeated crystal scattering and thermal motion. This is a point-scatterer model under the Born approximation, not a claim about the scattering strengths of named elements. Its crystal basis structure factor is
Fhkl​(u)=1+0.6e2πihu,Jhkl​(u)=∣Fhkl​(u)∣2=1.36+1.2cos(2πhu).
(5)
Here J is a dimensionless squared motif amplitude. Comparing it with measured integrated wave intensities requires the experimental geometry and detector response as well. The algebra follows directly by multiplying F by its complex conjugate; the cross term records wave interference between the two sites.
With u=1/2, reflections with even h have J=2.56, whereas odd h gives J=0.16, a ratio of 16:1. With u=1/4, the first four (h00) values instead are 1.36,0.16,1.36,2.56. Their geometrically possible positions are unchanged, although their strengths change. For equal stipulated amplitudes fA​=fB​=1 and u=1/2, the odd-h amplitude vanishes exactly: an example of a systematic absence. Different motif weights can thus expose a repeat that equal weights conceal.
The same formula also proves an ambiguity: u=1/4 and u=3/4 give identical Jhkl​ for every integer h,k,l, because cos(2πh(1−u))=cos(2πhu). Yet F100​ changes from 1+0.6i to 1−0.6i, reversing its wave phase. This particular ambiguity is inversion of the motif; it does not prove that these two simple motifs are distinct chemical substances. The conclusion is conditional on the stipulated real scattering amplitudes.
Phase problem
Words: 122
X-ray crystallographic structure inference OurBigBook.com
The phase problem is the loss of the wave phases of the crystal basis structure factors when an experiment records their squared magnitudes. Write Fhkl​=∣Fhkl​∣eiϕhkl​. A Fourier series reconstruction of a periodic electron density uses both ∣Fhkl​∣ and ϕhkl​, whereas an ordinary wave intensity measurement supplies only ∣Fhkl​∣2. Estimating the missing phases therefore needs additional constraints or measurements.[ref]
There is also an unavoidable choice of origin. Translating all motif positions by the same fractional crystal coordinate vector t multiplies Fhkl​ by e2πi(h,k,l)⋅t without changing ∣Fhkl​∣2. The physical arrangement is unchanged. A reconstructed coordinate list must therefore distinguish a coordinate convention from information actually recovered from the measurements.
Bragg structure inference from measured intensities
Words: 170
X-ray crystallographic structure inference OurBigBook.com
William Lawrence Bragg's 1913 structure paper connects a slit-selected beam, an oriented crystal and an ionization chamber to strength-versus-angle curves. Repeated sine ratios and matching absorption coefficients identify common radiation. Narrower slits resolve blended lines. Absolute wavelengths remain undetermined there; intercrystal comparisons first give relative scales. The Bragg crystal reflection experiment of 1913 covers the alignment controls.[ref]
William Henry Bragg's 1915 Bakerian lecture, X-rays and Crystal Structure, separates the geometric and intensity arguments. Its Figure 9 compares reflection positions and strengths from three sodium chloride orientations; odd and even diffraction orders differ in strength along one orientation. The interpretation uses alternating scattering layers. Later, the calcite example identifies an internal oxygen coordinate that symmetry alone cannot fix. Improved wave intensity measurements revise a previously rough estimate. Thus a lattice assignment can precede determination of positions inside the unit cell; intensity interpretation also has experimental and theoretical limits. This is the father's 1915 lecture, distinct from the joint 1913 reflection paper.[ref]

Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
A lattice plane is a plane containing a two-dimensional periodic array of lattice points. Parallel lattice planes form equally spaced geometrical sheets; an atomic basis can place chemical atoms between them.
With primitive lattice translation vectors ai​, write r=xa1​+ya2​+za3​. For integers h,k,l with greatest common divisor one, the plane equations
hx+ky+lz=m,m∈Z,
(6)
give a complete family labeled by Miller indices (hkl). In a primitive cubic lattice, (110) means x+y=m, parallel to a3​.[ref]

Interplanar spacing (d)

Words: 202
Lattice plane OurBigBook.com
The interplanar spacing d is the perpendicular distance between parallel planes in a specified family. Measuring along an oblique line gives a larger distance, so the direction of measurement matters.
There is a short reciprocal lattice derivation. With the angular convention ai​⋅bj​=2πδij​, put G=hb1​+kb2​+lb3​. Then G⋅r=2πm is the same plane equation as hx+ky+lz=m. Thus G is a normal vector. Moving between consecutive sheets along this normal changes the dot product by 2π, giving
∣G∣d=2π,d=∣G∣2π​.
(7)
For perpendicular cubic axes of length a, this becomes
G=a2π​(h,k,l),dhkl​=h2+k2+l2​a​.
(8)
For example, choose a primitive cubic lattice with a=0.600nm. Its (210) lattice planes have d210​=0.600/5​≃0.268328nm. This is a chosen geometry, not an experimental value. The distance from a point to a plane gives the same result: the planes 2X+Y=0 and 2X+Y=a in ordinary Cartesian length coordinates are separated by a/5​.
Specify whether dhkl​ denotes spacing between successive occupied lattice planes or the formal spacing assigned to a reflection label. In a primitive cubic lattice, (200) has formal spacing a/2 but every other sheet contains no lattice points; its reflection is the second diffraction order of (100). In a face-centered cubic lattice with conventional cubic axes, the (200) sheets at half-integer X/a do contain lattice points. Here a/2 is the actual spacing of the complete family perpendicular to that cube edge. The Primitive cubic Bragg peak positions example explains how to avoid counting a reflection twice.

Words: 207 Articles: 2
Lattice plane OurBigBook.com
Three Miller indices (hkl) specify a lattice plane orientation in chosen unit cell axes. Choose a parallel plane away from the origin, express its intercepts in axis units, take reciprocals, and clear fractions. An infinite intercept gives index zero; a negative intercept gives a negative index, written with an overbar.[ref]
For example, intercepts (2a,3b,∞) have reciprocal ratios (1/2,1/3,0), so the orientation is (320) after multiplying by six. Relative to the same axes, intercepts (a,−b,∞) give (11ˉ0). Choosing a different parallel member changes the common intercept scale, not the orientation.
Primitive axes require relatively prime Miller indices for complete families. Centered conventional unit cells need not, as the FCC lattice (200) example shows. Reflection labels can also retain higher diffraction orders. Use the reciprocal lattice for the normal vector with oblique axes; the direct vector ha1​+ka2​+la3​ need not be perpendicular.

Miller index OurBigBook.com
Four hexagonal crystallographic plane indices (hkil) with i=−(h+k); the basal plane is (0001).

Words: 42
Miller index OurBigBook.com
A lattice direction [uvw] lies parallel to a plane (hkl) exactly when hu+kv+lw=0. Indeed, their direct and reciprocal lattice vectors have dot product proportional to this expression. This statement holds for noncubic cells as well; angles between directions still require the direct-lattice metric tensor.

Atomic basis of a crystal ({(sj​,rj​)}j=1N​)

Words: 492 Articles: 2
Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
An atomic basis of a crystal is the motif of chemical species sj​ and relative positions rj​ attached identically to every lattice point R of a Bravais lattice Λ. The ideal periodic structure is the labeled set
{(sj​,R+rj​):R∈Λ,j=1,…,N}.
(9)
The primitive lattice translation vectors generate R by integer combinations; the atomic basis lists what is repeated at R. These are different meanings of the word basis. In particular, the offsets rj​ need not be linearly independent vectors, and one of them may be zero. A primitive unit cell represents N motif sites, even though it represents only one lattice point.
Changing the origin, choosing another primitive unit cell, or moving a motif site by a Bravais lattice translation changes the coordinates used to describe the same infinite crystal structure. The grouping into a motif does not, by itself, identify bonded molecules. In solid sodium chloride, grouping one sodium cation and one chlorine anion into an atomic basis does not create a collection of discrete NaCl molecules; the ionic crystal has an extended network of equivalent neighboring ions.

Fractional crystal coordinate ((u,v,w))

Words: 75
Atomic basis of a crystal OurBigBook.com
Fractional crystal coordinates are the dimensionless coefficients in r=ua1​+va2​+wa3​ for specified unit cell vectors. They are not Cartesian lengths unless the vectors themselves are included. With primitive vectors, replacing u,v,w by values differing by integers selects an equivalent position in another unit cell.
In the two-dimensional example under crystal structure, B has position (0.65,0.55) in ordinary length coordinates, but fractional crystal coordinates (0.65/2,0.55/1.5)=(13/40,11/30). Multiplying these coefficients by the two translation vectors recovers the drawn position. Reporting the axes is therefore part of reporting a structure.

NaCl conventional cell and coordination

Words: 276
Atomic basis of a crystal OurBigBook.com
Ordinary solid sodium chloride has the rock salt structure. Choose a conventional cube of side a with chlorine anions at the corners and face centers, and sodium cations at the edge centers and cube center. Corner sites are shared by eight cubes, face sites by two and edge sites by four. The unit cell counts are therefore
NCl−​=8(81​)+6(21​)=4,NNa+​=12(41​)+1=4.
(10)
There are four formula units per conventional unit cell, rather than four separate NaCl molecules.[ref]
The Bravais lattice is a face-centered cubic lattice. One choice of primitive lattice translation vectors and atomic basis is
a1​=2a​(0,1,1),a2​=2a​(1,0,1),a3​=2a​(1,1,0),rCl−​=0,rNa+​=2a​(1,0,0).
(11)
The determinant gives a primitive unit cell volume of a3/4; that cell represents one cation and one anion. Four such volumes make the conventional cube. The union of all ion positions resembles a primitive cubic lattice of step a/2 only if the chemical labels are discarded: translation by a(1,0,0)/2 exchanges unlike ions and fails to preserve the chemical structure.
Each ion has six nearest unlike neighbors at distance a/2, along the positive and negative directions of the three cube axes. Thus the coordination number is six. Within either same-species face-centered cubic lattice, the nearest same-ion neighbors instead number twelve: their displacements are permutations of (±a/2,±a/2,0), all of length a/2​. Since a/2​>a/2, those twelve are a more distant shell in the complete sodium chloride structure. The number twelve describes the same-ion FCC lattice neighborhood; six describes the nearest unlike-ion neighborhood.

Crystal structure OurBigBook.com
The characteristic outward shape of a crystal; distinct from its internal crystal structure.

Adsorption

Words: 2k Articles: 26
Physical chemistry OurBigBook.com
Adsorption is accumulation of a substance at an interface. Binding a solute to a packing surface can delay its passage through a chromatography column. Ideal size-exclusion chromatography separates through SEC pore access without such binding; extra retention from adsorption requires a different interpretation.
For a gas contacting a solid, adsorption concentrates molecules at the boundary; absorption takes material into the bulk. A porous solid can have a large internal surface area: binding on pore walls is still adsorption, even though those walls lie inside the particle. Both processes can occur together. Desorption returns adsorbed material to the surrounding phase. The useful question is therefore not just how much material disappeared from the gas, but where it went and whether it returns when the pressure falls.
An adsorption site model turns this spatial distinction into counting. With twelve identical adsorption sites and three bound molecules, the surface coverage is θ=3/12=1/4. Filling six gives θ=1/2; filling twelve gives a complete monolayer. These are configurations illustrating the count, rather than measured arrangements or claims that all real surfaces have twelve sites.

The time dependence of an effluent concentration as retention capacity is approached or exhausted. Its early tail matters when a minimum retention time is required.

The translational Helmholtz free energy cost of restricting a dilute ideal gas from a volume V to an area A at the same temperature. For identical particle number and mass,
F2D​−F3D​=−NkB​TlnV/Λ3A/Λ2​=NkB​TlnAΛV​.
(12)
Here Λ is the thermal de Broglie wavelength. This contribution is positive for V/A≫Λ; a favourable binding energy must be added separately to predict net adsorption.

An ideal column model with the same adsorption-to-desorption ratio at every height. With x=Kp, the stationary height distribution is P(j)=(1−x)xj for 0≤x<1, and its mean is x/(1−x). Unlimited height makes the mean diverge as x→1−; at x≥1 no normalized equilibrium height distribution exists.

The interfacial excess of a species relative to bulk reference phases extrapolated up to a chosen reference surface. An excess number density per area is denoted Γ; its molar counterpart is Γ/NA​. When an interface is dominated by a molecular layer, an effective area per adsorbed molecule is Σ=1/Γ. The reference-surface convention matters in multicomponent systems.

Adsorption OurBigBook.com
An adsorption site is a position or local environment at which a chemical species can be retained at a boundary. Treating all adsorption sites as identical is an assumption about their binding properties, not a definition of adsorption.

In a one-molecule-per-adsorption site description, surface coverage is θ=Noccupied​/Nsites​, with 0≤θ≤1. For a macroscopic sample at chemical equilibrium, θ usually denotes the mean occupied fraction. Inferring it from total uptake also requires the capacity of a complete monolayer.

Adsorption OurBigBook.com
A monolayer is a single layer of chemical atoms or molecules. In the Langmuir adsorption model, a complete monolayer occupies every adsorption site; partial surface coverage leaves vacancies within that first layer. One layer need not mean one molecule per surface chemical atom.

Adsorption OurBigBook.com
An adsorption isotherm relates equilibrium uptake to surrounding pressure or concentration at fixed temperature. For a gas, specify the partial pressure of the adsorbing chemical species. An uptake trace during incomplete equilibration need not be an adsorption isotherm.

Adsorption isotherm OurBigBook.com
For the simple one-solute interface convention, surface excess per molecule is related to the derivative of surface tension γ with respect to the logarithm of solute activity a by the displayed equation. For ideal dilute behavior one may use concentration ratios in place of activity ratios. In molar units, Γmol​=−(RT)−1dγ/dlna. A local molecular area estimate is Σ=−kB​T/(dγ/dlna). Ionic surfactants can require counterion and activity factors; the simple single-component expression must not be transferred to them without specifying those constraints.

Langmuir adsorption model (θ=bP/(1+bP))

Words: 852 Articles: 7
Adsorption isotherm OurBigBook.com
Consider an ideal gas in chemical equilibrium with homogeneous, identical adsorption sites at fixed temperature. Each intact molecule occupies one site; only one monolayer is allowed. Occupation of distinct sites is independent: neighboring bound molecules do not change binding or release rates. The simplest Langmuir adsorption model has one adsorbing chemical species, no splitting of molecules, and no competitors. Irving Langmuir's 1918 paper treats simple adsorption alongside more complicated cases; its scope exceeds this particular model.[ref]
The derivation is a balance between arrivals finding vacancies and departures from occupied adsorption sites. Let ka​P be the arrival-and-binding rate per vacant site and kd​ the departure rate per occupied site. Thus ka​ has units of inverse pressure per unit time, whereas kd​ has units of inverse time. The mean surface coverage obeys
dtdθ​=ka​P(1−θ)−kd​θ.
(13)
At chemical equilibrium, setting the two terms equal gives
ka​P(1−θ)=kd​θ,b=kd​ka​​,θ=1+bPbP​​.
(14)
The product bP is dimensionless. Here P is the adsorbing gas's partial pressure, expressed in modern bar, with 1bar=105Pa, and b is expressed in bar−1. The pascal is the SI unit of pressure. This dimensional b is not itself a dimensionless thermodynamic equilibrium constant. A larger b gives greater surface coverage at the same P and temperature, but does not specify how quickly chemical equilibrium is reached: multiplying both rate coefficients by the same factor leaves b unchanged.
Choose b=0.5, 2, and 8bar−1 as illustrative parameters at one fixed temperature, without assigning a particular material. At P=0.5bar, substitution gives, respectively,
θ=1.250.25​=51​,θ=21​,θ=54​.
(15)
Solving θ=1/2 gives P1/2​=1/b: the three half-occupation pressures are 2, 0.5, and 0.125bar. For b=2bar−1, reaching θ=0.9 instead requires bP=9, or P=4.5bar. If the complete-monolayer capacity is stipulated to be qm​=10mmolg−1, then q=qm​θ predicts q=5mmolg−1 at P=0.5bar. This last number is an original hypothetical example, not a measured uptake.
The shape follows directly from the finite number of adsorption sites. For bP≪1, θ≈bP: nearly every arriving molecule finds a vacancy. For bP≫1, 1−θ=1/(1+bP)≈1/(bP): vacancies become scarce. More formally,
dPdθ​=(1+bP)2b​>0,dP2d2θ​=−(1+bP)32b2​<0.
(16)
Thus surface coverage rises with diminishing slope and approaches one only as P→∞. This saturation is a site-capacity limit, not a claim that the gas has reached its condensation pressure. A second layer, different site binding strengths, interactions between bound molecules, or a changing surface invalidate parts of the setup. A good fit alone does not establish identical adsorption sites: a restricted pressure range can hide such differences. The Langmuir adsorption model is useful because it makes the capacity and the pressure scale of filling separate, testable quantities.
Vibrational factor in a Langmuir equilibrium constant (bs​(T)=zs​(T)λ3eϵ/(kB​T)/(kB​T))

Langmuir adsorption model OurBigBook.com
Equating the site chemical potential with that of an internally structureless classical vapour gives θ=bs​p/(1+bs​p). The coefficient bs​ includes the bound vibrational partition factor, the translational thermal de Broglie wavelength, and the positive binding Boltzmann factor. It has inverse-pressure units. Half coverage occurs at p=1/bs​; an unspecified zs​(T) prevents a numerical pressure scale, but not the functional isotherm.

Langmuir adsorption model OurBigBook.com
An independent site has one empty state and an occupied set with binding energy −ϵ and vibrational partition function zs​. Its occupied probability is θ=zs​eβ(μ+ϵ)/[1+zs​eβ(μ+ϵ)]. The denominator enforces the one-molecule-per-site constraint even though the vapour may obey classical statistics. Multiple occupancy or lateral interactions require a different model.

The occupied-to-vacant probability ratio of the adsorption-site grand partition function is θ/(1−θ)=zs​eβ(μs​+ϵ). Taking its logarithm yields the displayed chemical potential. binding energy and vibrational energies must share a consistent reference so that zero-point energy is not counted twice.

Langmuir adsorption model OurBigBook.com
The chemical potential of an ideal single-occupancy lattice gas with occupied-site internal partition function z and surface coverage θ. The ratio θ/(1−θ) accounts for the entropy of distributing particles among occupied and vacant adsorption sites.

Langmuir adsorption model OurBigBook.com
For independent spin-one-half adsorbates whose two spin states are split only at the surface, the one-site partition function contains 2cosh(μB​B/kB​T). Relative to the unsplit bulk spin degeneracy, this increases the Langmuir adsorption model affinity by a hyperbolic-cosine factor. At fixed temperature and gas pressure, increasing the magnitude of the magnetic field increases surface coverage in this model.
Competitive adsorption
Words: 61
Langmuir adsorption model OurBigBook.com
Competitive adsorption occurs when different chemical species seek the same adsorption sites. For intact molecules A and B, retain identical adsorption sites and no interactions, but replace the vacant fraction by 1−θA​−θB​. The same equilibrium balance gives
θA​=1+bA​PA​+bB​PB​bA​PA​​,θB​=1+bA​PA​+bB​PB​bB​PB​​.
(17)
Here PA​ and PB​ are partial pressures, not total pressure. Increasing PB​ can reduce θA​ at unchanged PA​: replacing PA​ by total pressure in a single-species Langmuir isotherm loses this competition.
Dissociative adsorption
Words: 90
Langmuir adsorption model OurBigBook.com
In dissociative adsorption, an arriving molecule splits into bound fragments. For the idealized process A2​+2∗⇌2A∗, let ∗ denote a vacant adsorption site and let θ count sites occupied by A. A mean-field approximation with independent vacancies takes the forward rate proportional to P(1−θ)2 and the reverse rate proportional to θ2. Equating them yields
1−θθ​=KP​,θ=1+KP​KP​​,
(18)
with a positive coefficient K of inverse-pressure units that includes the chosen pair-counting convention. This square-root dependence illustrates why the intact-molecule Langmuir isotherm cannot simply be assumed for splitting molecules. Requirements for neighboring vacancies or interactions can further change the mean-field approximation.

Langmuir mica adsorption experiment

Words: 163
Adsorption OurBigBook.com
In 1918, Irving Langmuir measured adsorption using freshly split mica strips, handled at their edges, separated by iron spacers and held with brass fasteners. A glass bulb contained the bundle; a similar blank contained matching iron and brass but no mica. Evacuated glass connections, Mercury seals, liquid air traps, and McLeod gauges provided controlled gas handling. Calibrated compartment volumes and pressure readings before and after expansion gave free-gas amounts; their deficit indicated uptake. Lowering pressure and measuring released gas tested desorption.[ref]
Hydrogen blank runs calibrated cooling-related pressure differences. Irving Langmuir pre-cooled the bulbs to reduce thermal delay; he suggested slow diffusion between strips could control the remaining approach to equilibrium. Critically, blank uptake was not subtracted: he estimated the mica-bulb results were 10–30% too high. Liquid air temperature drift was unrecorded. These limits constrain inference of intrinsic binding from the uptake curve. The paper's pressure unit called “bar” was 1dyncm−2=0.1Pa, unlike the modern bar used above.[ref]

Absorption (chemistry)

Words: 44
Physical chemistry OurBigBook.com
Absorption takes a chemical substance into a material's bulk, as when carbon dioxide dissolves in water. Adsorption instead concerns accumulation at a boundary. Bulk uptake and interfacial accumulation can coexist; total uptake alone does not separate their contributions. This use of absorption concerns material uptake, whereas absorbance describes attenuation of electromagnetic radiation.

Chemical polarity

Words: 94 Articles: 2
Physical chemistry OurBigBook.com
Chemical polarity concerns unequal distribution of electron density in a chemical bond or molecule. A polar molecule has a permanent electric dipole moment; the effects of individual bonds must be combined with their spatial arrangement. In a symmetric linear carbon dioxide molecule, opposing bond-dipole contributions cancel. In water, its bent molecular geometry prevents that cancellation, giving a permanent electric dipole moment.[ref]

Polar molecule

Words: 24
Chemical polarity OurBigBook.com
A polar molecule has a nonzero permanent electric dipole moment because of its internal electric charge distribution. It can still have zero total electric charge. Water is polar; a nonpolar molecule has no permanent electric dipole moment.

Nonpolar molecule

Words: 19
Chemical polarity OurBigBook.com
A nonpolar molecule has no permanent electric dipole moment. This distinguishes its charge distribution from the separated partial charges of a polar molecule.

Hydrophilicity

Words: 59
Physical chemistry OurBigBook.com
Hydrophilicity describes affinity for water. Regions with chemical polarity or electric charge can interact favorably with water, including through hydrogen bonds where suitable groups are present. Hydrophilic regions of membrane-forming phospholipids face the water on either side of a lipid bilayer. Such affinity does not mean forming covalent bonds with every neighboring substance, nor does it require a net negative electric charge. See Alberts et al.: the chemical components of a cell.

Amphiphile

Words: 600 Articles: 10
Physical chemistry OurBigBook.com
An amphiphile is a molecule containing distinct hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions. Amphiphilic and amphipathic describe this combination. Membrane-forming phospholipids are examples; their two regions give different parts of one molecule different affinities for water. The word describes a structure, not a guarantee of a particular aggregate shape. See IUPAC Gold Book: amphiphilic.

Micelle

Words: 555 Articles: 9
Amphiphile OurBigBook.com
A micelle is a finite aggregate of amphiphiles in a solvent. In an ordinary aqueous micelle, hydrophobic tails occupy the interior and hydrophilic heads contact the surrounding water. Association can lower the Gibbs free energy by reducing unfavorable tail exposure, despite loss of molecular translational entropy. Head-group interactions and chain packing help select the aggregate size and shape. A micelle has a filled tail-rich core, unlike a lipid vesicle with a solvent-filled interior bounded by a lipid bilayer.

Cylindrical micelle geometry (R=2v/a0​)

Words: 44
Micelle OurBigBook.com
For a long cylindrical micelle with negligible end caps, incompressible tail volume v and head-group area a0​ give v/a0​=R/2. The geometric requirement R≤ℓc​ bounds the amphiphile packing parameter by 1/2. The conventional cylindrical range is approximately 1/3≲v/(a0​ℓc​)≲1/2; aggregate transitions also depend on interactions and chain conformations.

Aggregation number (Nagg​)

Micelle OurBigBook.com
The number of constituent molecules in an aggregate. An observed population generally has a distribution of aggregation numbers.

Spherical micelle geometry (R=3v/a0​,n=36πv2/a03​)

Micelle OurBigBook.com
In a sharp-core spherical micelle of aggregation number n, incompressible tail volume v per molecule and effective head-group area a0​ give nv=4πR3/3 and na0​=4πR2. Division gives the displayed radius and aggregation number. If the maximum tail extension is lc​, the model requires R≤lc​, equivalently the amphiphile packing parameter v/(a0​lc​)≤1/3. Input dimensions violating that inequality cannot describe an exact spherical filled core without modifying the molecular geometry assumptions.

Amphiphile packing parameter (P=v/(a0​ℓ))

Words: 112
Micelle OurBigBook.com
For an amphiphile, let v be its hydrophobic-tail volume, a0​ its effective head-group area, and ℓ its maximum tail extension. The dimensionless packing parameter P=v/(a0​ℓ) estimates compatible aggregate curvature. For a spherical micelle of core radius r containing n molecules, nv=4πr3/3 and na0​=4πr2, giving v/a0​=r/3. Since r≤ℓ, spherical packing requires P≤1/3. The analogous long-cylinder calculation gives v/a0​=r/2 and the limiting value 1/2; a planar monolayer has v/a0​ equal to its thickness and limiting value one. Thus small P favors spherical micelles, intermediate values favor cylindrical aggregates, and values near one favor lipid bilayers. This is a geometric guide, not a full thermodynamic prediction of every phase boundary.

Micelle OurBigBook.com
The critical micelle concentration is the approximate surfactant concentration above which additional dissolved amphiphile predominantly enters micelles rather than remaining as isolated molecules. It is a concentration crossover governed by equality of the molecular chemical potential in the two environments, not a claim that absolutely no aggregates exist below a sharp threshold. Temperature, ionic conditions and molecular structure affect its value.

This gives x1,∗​≃exp[(μ∗0​−μ10​)/(kB​T)] in the large-aggregation approximation. A minimum of the aggregate free-energy balance at a finite size produces a micellar population around that size, in addition to monomers. Hydrophobicity

Words: 194 Articles: 2
Physical chemistry OurBigBook.com
Hydrophobicity describes unfavorable mixing with water, as illustrated by long hydrocarbon regions. The hydrophobic regions of membrane-forming phospholipids face the interior of a lipid bilayer. This organization is explained by the hydrophobic effect, rather than by imagining that chains actively repel water. See IUPAC Gold Book: hydrophobic interaction.

Hydrophobic effect

Words: 151 Articles: 1
Hydrophobicity OurBigBook.com
The hydrophobic effect is the solvent-mediated tendency of nonpolar regions to associate in water. Exposing a hydrocarbon region changes how surrounding water molecules can arrange and interact; reducing that exposure can lower the total free energy. Both water and lipids enter the accounting. The effect is not an additional covalent bond between chains. See IUPAC Gold Book: hydrophobic interaction.
At fixed temperature and pressure, compare two candidate organizations by the change in Gibbs free energy, ΔG=ΔH−TΔS, where H is enthalpy, T is absolute temperature, and S is entropy. An organization with lower G is favored in this comparison. Reducing exposed hydrocarbon area is one contribution; changes in chain packing and the entropy of the lipids also matter. This explains why hydrophobicity alone cannot predict every aggregate shape. See 16.4 Free Energy.

Hydrophobic attraction

Words: 35
Hydrophobic effect OurBigBook.com
A solvent-mediated tendency of appropriately prepared water-repelling surfaces to associate. Surface chemistry, dissolved gas and the experimental geometry can strongly affect the measured force; it is not a universal replacement for every other colloidal interaction.

Absorbance (A)

Words: 1k Articles: 5
Physical chemistry OurBigBook.com
Absorbance is the dimensionless quantity A=log10​(P0​/P), where P0​ and P are reference and transmitted radiant powers at the chosen wavelength. For example, A=1 means one tenth of the reference power is transmitted. Under the Beer-Lambert law, absorbance can determine an absorbing species' concentration; attenuation by cloudiness or unrelated colored solutes needs separate controls. [ref]

Beer-Lambert law (A=εlc)

Words: 1k Articles: 4
Absorbance OurBigBook.com
The Beer-Lambert law relates absorbance A to an absorbing species' concentration c and path length l by A=εlc in a homogeneous medium using sufficiently narrow-band light. The coefficient ε depends on the species, wavelength and chemical solution conditions. This makes Ellman's reagent useful for quantitative thiol assays once its released colored species has been calibrated. [ref]
Here c is molar concentration, l is the geometric length through the sample, and ε is the molar absorption coefficient. The ideal beam has parallel light rays, a single wavelength, and a medium with uniform composition and isotropy; finite spectral width must be small relative to features in the optical spectrum.[ref]
For a spectrophotometer, distinguish the source's output from the reference that reaches the photodetector. Let P0​ be the received radiant power through a reference blank and P the received radiant power through the sample, after subtracting the photodetector's dark response. Both refer to the same selected wavelength band and collection geometry. Define the blank-normalized transmittance and absorbance by
T=P0​P​,A=−log10​T,T=10−A.
(19)
The reference blank includes the solvent and other assay ingredients except the absorbing target. Matching cuvettes and conditions makes their common losses divide out. Thus this T is relative to the reference blank; it is not the absolute transmittance of the entire cuvette and its contents. Both radiant powers can be expressed in watts, while their ratio, T, and its logarithm, A, are dimensionless. An instrument displaying 40% transmission means T=0.40, not T=40.
Why take a logarithm? Consider two consecutive identical absorbing layers. Each transmits a fraction t of the radiant power entering it, so together they transmit t2. Their absorbances add because −log10​(t2)=2(−log10​t). Doubling the sample length doubles absorbance while squaring transmittance. This turns multiplicative loss into an additive scale and makes a straight line useful for inferring molar concentration.
A short model derivation makes the assumption explicit. Suppose a thin layer of thickness dx removes the fraction kcdx of its incoming radiant power, where k is a fixed constant of proportionality and c is a uniform molar concentration. The corresponding ordinary differential equation, initial condition, and solution are
dxdP​=−kcP,P(0)=P0​,P(l)=P0​e−kcl.
(20)
Taking the base-ten logarithm gives A=kcl/ln10, so ε=k/ln10. The exponential decay follows from equal layers removing equal fractions of what remains. Proportionality to molar concentration additionally assumes that the absorbing chemical species retains the same response as its molar concentration changes; the geometric argument alone does not establish that.

Beer-Lambert law OurBigBook.com
The decadic molar absorption coefficient specifies absorbance per geometric length and molar concentration. With l in centimetres and c in molL−1, ε has units Lmol−1cm−1; its SI unit is m2mol−1.[ref]
The units cancel in εlc. Since 1L=10−3m3 and 1cm=10−2m, one Lmol−1cm−1 equals 0.1m2mol−1. Specify the wavelength and chemical solution conditions when giving a molar absorption coefficient: changing the absorbing chemical species can change it even at fixed total analytical concentration.
