A micromolar molar concentration is 1μM=10−6molL−1, so each additional 25μM gives ΔA=8000×1×25×10−6=0.2. Five chosen standards therefore predict
c(μM)AT​001​250.20.63096​500.40.39811​750.60.25119​1000.80.15849​
(21)
The absorbance graph is a straight line of slope 0.008(μM)−1, while the transmittance graph shows exponential decay. Equal increments of molar concentration multiply transmittance by 10−0.2≈0.63096; they do not subtract a fixed transmitted fraction.
Suppose a measurement returns the stipulated blank-normalized reading T=0.40 under those same conditions. The inferred absorbance and molar concentration are
A=−log10​(0.40)=log10​(2.5)≈0.3979400,c=8000×1log10​(2.5)​molL−1≈49.7425μM.
(22)
This lies slightly below the 50μM standard because 0.40 is slightly above 10−0.4≈0.39811. A calibration determined experimentally by linear regression may instead have A=mc+b. Then use c=(A−b)/m, keeping the slope m and intercept b in their measured units. A nonzero intercept calls for checking the reference blank and sample preparation; it does not uniquely identify the cause.

Beer-Lambert measurement controls

Words: 440 Articles: 1
Beer-Lambert law OurBigBook.com
An actual teaching experiment prepares a Kool-Aid stock by weighing powder, transferring it quantitatively into a volumetric flask, and filling to the mark with water. A Genesys 30 spectrophotometer, blanked with water in a cuvette, scans for the peak absorbance wavelength. A Genesys 10 then measures absorbance at that wavelength, with a water reference blank. Each serial dilution transfers 50mL of the preceding chemical solution to a 100mL volumetric flask and fills to the mark; the protocol records the blank and sample readouts and repeats the halving sequence. These are prescribed experimental steps, not a published numerical data set.[ref]
The experiment tests whether absorbance tracks the prepared concentration. Its concentration is powder mass per final volume, so the calibration does not by itself supply a single dye's molar absorption coefficient. The manual identifies loss of discrimination for very concentrated, very dilute, or very similar samples.[ref]
To interpret such a calibration, hold cuvette orientation fixed with its clear faces in the light path, keep fingerprints and bubbles out of that path, and keep the geometric length unchanged. Mix each dilution completely. Re-read the reference blank during the sequence and re-read one standard to test drift. A separate preparation of a standard checks errors propagated through serial dilution; repeating only its instrumental reading does not test the transferred volumes. These controls follow from keeping P0​, l, and c comparable between readings.
Three mechanisms explain why a straight line can fail. First, scattering of light can divert radiant power away from the photodetector, so cloudiness can raise apparent absorbance without the intended absorbing solute. A reference blank removes only losses shared with the sample. Second, stray light reaching the photodetector can make a strongly absorbing sample appear too transmissive. In an original model with extra detected radiant power sP0​ in both readings,
Tread​=1+s10−εlc+s​,Aread​=−log10​Tread​.
(23)
As the ideal transmittance approaches zero, the reported absorbance approaches log10​((1+s)/s) for s>0. This finite ceiling is a model prediction, not measured instrument performance.
Third, chemical equilibrium can redistribute the absorbing chemical species when dilution, pH, or temperature changes. Even if each chemical species separately follows the Beer-Lambert law, their combined absorbance is A=l∑i​εi​ci​, where ci​ is each species' molar concentration; changing those fractions need not preserve one effective molar absorption coefficient. Thus an unknown should be compared with standards under matching chemical solution conditions, within the tested concentration range. A good linear regression alone does not establish chemical selectivity.
Reference blank
Words: 37
Beer-Lambert measurement controls OurBigBook.com
A reference blank is the comparison sample used to establish the background response in a measurement. For absorbance, it contains matching solvent and other assay ingredients without the target absorbing chemical species; it sets the reference radiant power P0​ under matching cuvette and wavelength conditions.

Photoemission spectroscopy

Words: 2k Articles: 14
Physical chemistry OurBigBook.com
Photoelectron spectroscopy measures the kinetic energies of photoelectrons produced by illuminating matter with photons of known energy. The photoelectric effect supplies the emission mechanism; spectroscopy turns the distribution of emitted electron energies into information about occupied energy levels and chemical bonds. A broad survey helps identify chemical elements, while small shifts within one element's lines can distinguish different chemical surroundings. These are different questions: finding carbon does not establish which chemical bonds its chemical atoms form.
The useful inversion is an energy balance. A known incoming photon energy pays for removal of an electron and for its outgoing kinetic energy. To apply that balance to a solid, specify the zero of energy and the work function of the instrument. Photoelectron binding energy reference derives the conversion for a conducting sample in electrical contact with its analyzer. A free molecule instead has an ionization energy referenced to an electron at rest in vacuum; it need not share a Fermi level with the analyzer.

Core-level chemical shift (ΔEB​)

Words: 41
Photoemission spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
A core-binding-energy difference associated with chemical environment, such as bonding to an adsorbate or a change of oxidation state. Comparisons require the same core-level branch and a common calibrated energy reference. Local electrostatics, hybridization and final-state core-hole screening can all contribute.

Surface core-level shift (ΔEB​=EBsurface​−EBbulk​)

Words: 56
Photoemission spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
A difference in the binding energy of the same core level for surface and bulk atoms of one material. Reduced coordination changes bonding and local potential; the relaxation that screens the photoemission core hole also changes. A measured shift combines these initial- and final-state effects and cannot by itself be converted into a unique local charge.

Ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy

Words: 22
Photoemission spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
photoelectron spectroscopy using ultraviolet photons to probe occupied electronic states, often valence states. Empty states above the Fermi level require a different measurement or deliberate population.

Concentric hemispherical electron analyser

Words: 75 Articles: 2
Photoemission spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
An electrostatic energy analyser using trajectories between two concentric hemispheres. electrons near a selected pass energy reach the exit aperture; entrance optics can retard faster electrons before analysis.

Electron analyser retard ratio

Words: 21
Concentric hemispherical electron analyser OurBigBook.com
The ratio of electron kinetic energy before retardation to hemispherical pass energy. This definition should be stated because a voltage-to-pass-energy ratio differs by one.

Electron analyser pass energy

Words: 28
Concentric hemispherical electron analyser OurBigBook.com
The kinetic energy selected in the hemispherical analysing field, distinguished from the kinetic energy before retarding entrance optics. At fixed geometry the absolute instrumental energy width is approximately proportional to pass energy.

Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy

Words: 246 Articles: 2
Photoemission spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy measures the kinetic energy and emission angle of electrons removed from a solid by light. With photon energy hν, sample work function Φ, and binding energy EB​ measured downwards from the Fermi level, Ekin​=hν−Φ−EB​. The measured parallel momentum is k∥​=2me​Ekin​​sinθ/ℏ, modulo a surface reciprocal-lattice vector. Bright ridges reveal occupied electronic band structure; their slopes give the corresponding group velocity. Extracting a Fermi energy relative to a Dirac point requires a calibrated Fermi level, not merely an unlabelled image boundary.

Photoemission momentum conversion (k∥​=2me​Ekin​​sinθ/ℏ)

Words: 95
Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
For emission angle θ measured from the surface normal, a free outgoing photoelectron has parallel wavevector k∥​=2me​Ekin​​sinθ/ℏ. Translation symmetry parallel to a clean periodic surface conserves this component modulo a surface reciprocal lattice vector, after accounting for photon momentum when needed. With initial binding energy EB​ below the Fermi level, its kinetic energy immediately outside the sample is Ekin​=hν−ϕs​−EB​, where ϕs​ is the sample work function. This sample-vacuum energy is distinct from the analyzer-referenced energy when contact potentials are present. Perpendicular crystal momentum generally needs a final-state model, whereas a strictly two-dimensional band has no perpendicular dispersion to reconstruct.

Photoemission intensity and spectral function (I(k,ϵ)∝∣M∣2f(ϵ)A(k,ϵ))

Words: 76
Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
Within the dipole and sudden approximation, angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy measures the electron removal spectral function multiplied by a transition matrix element. Finite instrumental energy and angular resolution convolve this product, and inelastic scattering adds a background. Peak positions reveal occupied electronic band structure, while intrinsic line widths contain lifetime information. Matrix elements depend on photon energy, polarization, orbital character, and geometry, so weak intensity does not by itself establish the absence of an electronic state. Equilibrium photoemission does not directly measure unoccupied bands far above the Fermi level.

X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy

Words: 1k Articles: 4
Photoemission spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy uses X-ray excitation to investigate electron removal energies, including those of core electrons. The common name electron spectroscopy for chemical analysis emphasizes its use in distinguishing chemical surroundings. The whole recorded spectrum can also contain electrons produced by processes other than direct photoionization; a peak assignment must identify the emission process as well as the chemical element.
In a modern implementation, a quartz crystal selects aluminum characteristic X-rays according to Bragg's law and focuses them onto the sample. Vacuum reduces gas collisions and contamination; a separately pumped entry chamber limits exposure to air. Lenses collect photoelectrons; an electrostatic electron energy analyzer transmits a narrow kinetic energy band. Stepping that band and counting detector pulses produces the spectrum. An electron flood source can compensate positive electric charge on insulating samples. Ion cleaning can alter vulnerable samples.[ref]
For a scan with count Nj​ and dwell time tj​ at setting j, compare rates Nj​/tj​, rather than raw counts when dwell times differ. Under an independent Poisson distribution model, the count standard deviation is approximately Nj​​ for a sufficiently populated bin. Longer acquisition reduces this relative counting measurement uncertainty; it does not automatically improve separation of overlapping peaks. Photoelectron peak overlap and resolution gives an example in which the same chemical separation produces either two maxima or one.

Photoelectron binding energy reference (EB​=hν−Ekin​−ϕanalyzer​)

Words: 409
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
Let a conducting sample and conducting analyzer be in good electrical contact, unbiased, at equilibrium, and without appreciable charging during illumination. Their Fermi levels then coincide. Choose that common Fermi level as zero. Define EB​>0 as the binding energy relative to this zero: removing an electron into the electron reservoir at the Fermi level costs EB​. It is not the cost of removing the electron all the way to the sample's vacuum level.
Write the sample and analyzer work functions as ϕs​ and ϕa​. Their local vacuum levels lie at ϕs​ and ϕa​ above the common Fermi level. Conservation of energy for an electron emitted without additional losses gives total outgoing energy hν−EB​, where h is the Planck constant and ν the photon frequency. Immediately outside the sample its kinetic energy is Ks​=hν−EB​−ϕs​. The contact-related electric potential changes this to
Ekin​=Ks​+ϕs​−ϕa​=hν−EB​−ϕa​,EB​=hν−Ekin​−ϕa​.
(24)
Thus the sample work function cancels when the measured kinetic energy is referenced to the analyzer. Substituting ϕs​ for ϕa​ in the final conversion would mix two different energy references. An instrument's calibrated binding energy scale can incorporate its effective analyzer work function, so the correction need not appear as a separate operator-entered number.
As an original numerical example, stipulate hν=1486.6eV, ϕa​=4.5eV and a line at EB​=284.0eV. The predicted analyzer kinetic energy is 1198.1eV. If ϕs​=5.0eV, the surface value is instead Ks​=1197.6eV; the contact-related increase is 0.5eV. A second line at 286.0eV gives 1196.1eV at the analyzer. A +2.0eV chemical shift in photoelectron spectroscopy therefore appears as a −2.0eV shift in measured kinetic energy. These are chosen values, not a measured carbon spectrum.
Charging breaks the assumed reference. If a uniformly charging sample rises by electric potential V>0 relative to the analyzer, an escaping electron loses an additional energy eV, with e the positive elementary charge. Applying the unbiased conversion consequently returns
EB,apparent​=EB,true​+eV.
(25)
Two features from the same stable potential retain their separation. Features from regions at different potentials acquire different offsets, which can mimic chemical differences or broaden a line. A conducting holder alone does not establish electrical contact through an insulating surface layer. Compare repeat scans, electrical contact and charge-compensation settings before interpreting an offset as a change in chemical bonds.
Measurement calibration is a separate issue: a known reference line tests the scale, while charge compensation controls the specimen's electric potential. In an original offset model EB,read​=EB,true​+b, one known line determines b. An unknown scale factor in EB,read​=aEB,true​+b requires two distinct known lines to determine both a and b. Re-reading a reference after a sample checks drift. Treating an unidentified contamination peak as a universally fixed reference would assume the chemical identity and electrical behavior that the measurement should test.

Chemical shift in photoelectron spectroscopy (ΔEB​)

Words: 587 Articles: 1
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
A chemical shift in photoelectron spectroscopy is a difference in binding energy for the same kind of core electron in different chemical surroundings, using comparable energy references. Identifying a chemical element assigns its family of lines; resolving chemical shifts within that family asks how its chemical atoms are bonded. For example, distinguishing a metal from its chemically modified surface requires more than detecting that element in both places.
The removal energy compares the initial electronic state with the state left after emission. Redistribution of the remaining electrons changes that final state's energy; a measured shift therefore includes relaxation as well as initial bonding effects.[ref]
This makes chemical shift in photoelectron spectroscopy useful but conditional. Compare the same electron shell, the same photoelectron binding energy reference, and compatible sample conditions. Agreement with a chemically appropriate reference supports an assignment; a line position by itself need not uniquely determine an oxidation state. An unresolved sum of two chemical components can even have a centroid where neither component lies. The following Gaussian mixture distribution shows exactly how that happens without claiming a material identification.
Photoelectron peak overlap and resolution
Words: 430
Chemical shift in photoelectron spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
Choose two hypothetical environments A and B of one chemical element, with line centers μA​=284eV and μB​=286eV. Model each line by a normalized Gaussian function with common standard deviation σ, and stipulate integrated count weights wA​=3/4, wB​=1/4. On the binding energy axis E, the normalized count density is
G(E;μ,σ)=2π​σ1​exp[−2σ2(E−μ)2​],I(E)=43​G(E;284,σ)+41​G(E;286,σ).
(26)
All energies in this expression use electronvolts. Each component's integrated area equals its count weight, and ∫I(E)dE=1. There is no background, statistical counting fluctuation, or additional emission feature in this stipulated model. These choices deliberately isolate photoelectron peak overlap and resolution.
Direct integration, or the law of total expectation applied to the component label, gives the centroid
Eˉ=wA​μA​+wB​μB​=284.5eV.
(27)
The centroid lies between the chemical environments and is not either component's binding energy. Expanding (E−Eˉ)2 within each component, the odd cross term integrates to zero. The resulting variance is
Var(E)=σ2+wA​wB​(μB​−μA​)2=σ2+0.75eV2.
(28)
For σ=0.25eV the variance is 0.8125eV2 and the two maxima are separated. For σ=1.00eV it is 1.7500eV2 and there is one maximum. Each Gaussian's full width at half maximum is 22ln2​σ, approximately 0.589 and 2.355eV respectively. The chemical separation remains 2eV in both cases. The number of visible maxima therefore does not equal the number of chemical components.
One interpretation of this change is additional independent Gaussian instrument blur. The convolution of probability densities adds the variances, so broadening σ=0.25 to 1 requires response standard deviation 1−0.252​=15​/4≃0.968246eV. A normalized response with zero mean preserves the centroid and integrated counts. Real line shapes and backgrounds can depart from this model, and separating hidden components is an inverse problem; a plausible fit does not alone establish uniqueness.
Finally, count weights describe detection. In a simple response model, let ni​ denote the number of emitting sites sampled in environment i, si​ its effective photoionization cross section, and Ti​ the probability that its emitted electron contributes to the selected measured line. Then
Ai​=Cni​si​Ti​,wi​=∑j​nj​sj​Tj​ni​si​Ti​​.
(29)
The common factor C includes exposure. Here Ti​ includes escape from the sample, analyzer transmission and detection. Count weights equal site fractions only if the relevant response factors are equal or corrected. They are not automatically molecular mole fractions; different molecules can supply different numbers of the selected emitting sites. In an original example, equal site numbers with sA​TA​=3sB​TB​ give the plotted 3:1 count ratio despite a 1:1 site ratio.

Siegbahn photoelectron spectroscopy experiments

Words: 140
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
Kai Siegbahn's early instrument used iron-free magnetic double focusing and a thin-window Geiger-Müller counter. His later instrument, compatible with ultra-high vacuum, used a spherical electrostatic electron energy analyzer and monochromatic aluminum X-rays. Argon mixed with methane supplied simultaneous 2p reference lines.[ref]
Two sulfur lines in sodium thiosulfate distinguished chemical environments within one compound. A separate gold comparison showed a fingerprint obscuring substrate lines.[ref]
For an unknown sample, first document its preparation and transfer, then compare survey and detailed scans under reproducible illumination, contact and acquisition conditions. Repeat a region to test change during exposure. If a cleaning treatment is used, compare before and after rather than assuming that cleaning preserves the original chemical bonds. Report the photoelectron binding energy reference, reference lines, charge-compensation conditions and instrumental settings with the inferred chemical shift in photoelectron spectroscopy. A chemical interpretation should survive these checks as well as explain the line separation.
